transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-05-19 15:30 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (StoneCove), Elena Morales (StoneCove), Tomás Ruiz (StoneCove)

Summary: quick discovery focused on private onramp to Redwood Private, VPC peering, private endpoints, and regional restrictions for EU data residency. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private; leaning to Private due to regulated workloads and internal SSO/KMS needs.

Topics: private endpoints, transit gateway, egress controls, KMS/HSM integration, SOC2/ISO evidence, pilot timeline, latency/cost tradeoffs

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood, ill kick us off. quick intro round?
[00:12] Raj (StoneCove): yeah hi, raj here, head of platform at stonecove. we've got compliance and some networking constraints so figured we should talk private onramp.
[00:18] Elena (StoneCove): elena, security architect; i'm mainly concerned about key management and auditability.
[00:22] Tomás (StoneCove): tomás, networking, i'll be the one poking at routing.
[00:27] Liam (Redwood SE): liam here, se — i'll cover the technical bits, latency, peering, etc.
[00:33] Maya (Redwood): great. objective for today — map your constraints and see how redwood private can fit: peering options, private endpoints, region gating, and the typical trade offs.
[00:45] Raj: yes, we have three must-haves: 1) EU-only data residency for inference payloads, 2) KMS integration with customer-managed keys, 3) no public egress from our VPC for model payloads.
[00:58] Maya (Redwood): makes sense. liam, can you talk through the private connectivity options?
[01:05] Liam (Redwood SE): sure. we generally support two patterns for private: VPC peering / transit via a transit-gateway, and private endpoint (privatelink style) where traffic terminates in our private plane. for larger scale, we recommend dedicated private deployments inside your account or a customer-managed VPC peering to our private endpoint.
[01:28] Tomás (StoneCove): when you say "private endpoint" do you expose an NLB inside our VPC or is it reverse? we can't accept inbound from public internet.
[01:35] Liam (Redwood SE): good question. for cloud providers we set up an interface endpoint inside your VPC — effectively a privatelink — so traffic stays within the backbone. there is no public ingress from the internet to that endpoint. for on-prem we provide a VPN/DirectConnect pattern.
[01:49] Elena (StoneCove): we need assurance that audit logs and request traces are preserved in our logging stack. can we push logs to our splunk or a SIEM?
[01:57] Maya (Redwood): yes, we have log forwarding integrations and can ship audit logs to your S3 or to a SIEM via a dedicated forwarder. we'll include details in the security pack.
[02:06] Raj: good. question on model KV cache and session state — does any customer data persist on the Redwood side? we need to know what touches redwood storage.
[02:16] Liam (Redwood SE): by default the runtime uses ephemeral memory and KV cache per model process; we don't persist raw user PII unless you opt into long-term storage like embeddings or metrics. for private deployments you can configure log retention and disable embeddings persistence; we can also run with customer-managed storage in your cloud account for some pieces.
[02:36] Speaker 1: mhm, okay.
[02:40] Raj: about regions — our EU legal requires that inference and ephemeral caches remain in eu-west-1 and eu-central-1 only. can you pin the model runner to specific regions?
[02:52] Liam (Redwood SE): yes, you can pin to region groups. in our Private product we can instantiate model shards in specific regions only. there are some caveats: if you request autoscaling we will only scale within pinned regions, which can affect burst capacity; we can discuss burst to dedicated in a secondary region if you need fallback.
[03:12] Elena: fallback is tricky because of legal. fallback to another EU region is okay but not to us-east.
[03:18] Maya (Redwood): noted, we can document the region gating policy in the SLOs.
[03:22] Tomás: what's the networking setup for NAT/egress? we're required to egress through our egress firewall for outbound calls, e.g., to a license server, and we need to control egress IPs.
[03:33] Liam (Redwood SE): for outbound egress from model containers you can route through your NAT gateway. in the privatelink pattern, most traffic is inbound from your VPC to redwood's endpoint, but any callbacks or external calls can be routed via your VPC egress if you host the model inside your account; if redwood hosts it in our infra we can offer static egress IPs via egress proxies located in the same region.
[03:56] Raj: static egress IPs are helpful. we also need TLS with client certs for mutual TLS to the endpoint. is that supported?
[04:03] Maya (Redwood): we support mTLS in Private via customer certs; we'll capture the cert rotation and CA process in the integration doc.
[04:10] Elena: KMS — can we use our AWS KMS or something on-prem HSM to wrap model keys?
[04:17] Liam: yes, customer-managed KMS is supported. for the most secure posture we recommend you keep root keys in your KMS/HSM and we use envelope encryption when we need to persist anything. we'll need an IAM role with kms:Decrypt permission for the service account.
[04:33] Raj: how about SSO and RBAC integration? we need SCIM and SAML + role mapping to separate dev/test from prod access.
[04:41] Maya (Redwood): we support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC can be tied to your groups; we will share the mapping guide.
[04:49] Tomás: latency — if we pin to eu-central, what network latency should we expect for typical 2-4k token responses?
[04:58] Liam: for models like our 13B quantized variants you should see p95 token latencies in the 70-120ms per-token range depending on batch size; network RTT will add so from inside eu-central you might add 5-15ms. we'll capture realistic perf numbers in the benchmark during the pilot.
[05:18] Raj: cost considerations, we're trying to decide between Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity vs Private in our VPC. what's the rough delta?
[05:27] Maya (Redwood): generally Dedicated is simpler operationally and cheaper per-token because we control the infra; Private has higher onboarding and egress considerations but gives you data isolation and control. pricing is dependent on commit levels; we'll surface a comparison sheet.
[05:39] Elena: security checklist — we need SOC2 type II report, encryption at rest, key rotation logs, and penetration test results.
[05:47] Maya (Redwood): yes we will include SOC2 and our pen test summary in the pack. some redwood infra references may be redacted for security.
[05:56] Raj: can we run a short pilot that only routes traffic from our non-prod env first?
[06:02] Maya (Redwood): absolutely. typical pilot is 1 week baseline benchmarks + a week of functional testing. we can do dev -> private endpoint first.
[06:11] Tomás: on the peering CIDR — our VPC is 10.10.0.0/16, we run a transit gateway; how does routing for keyboards — sorry for the phrase — for the endpoint look?
[06:23] Liam (Redwood SE): for privatelink we'll create interface endpoints in your subnets, so you won't need peering routes; for peering/transit you'll add a route to the model subnet pointing to our peer. with transit we just need the TGW attachment and prefix lists; we'll ask for your exact CIDRs.
[06:43] Speaker 2: quick interjection, do you support multi-tenant models in private?
[06:48] Liam (Redwood SE): yes but we strongly recommend single-tenant model runners for regulated data to avoid any co-tenancy surface. single-tenant has higher cost but better isolation.
[06:59] Raj: what about backups, are there any persisted checkpoints that could leave the region?
[07:05] Liam: backups are optional. if you enable them we will keep them in the pinned region or in your own S3 bucket if you prefer. we'll make sure any persisted artifacts are subject to the region policy.
[07:18] Maya: i'm going to note the risk areas: egress IPs, cert rotation, kms roles, and fallback region policy. we'll follow up with the security pack covering these.
[07:28] Elena: can you share the network diagram for the privatelink flow? we'd like to run a quick tabletop.
[07:35] Maya: yes — we'll share a diagram and a step-by-step onboarding checklist.
[07:40] Raj: how long to get a dev pilot up and running? assuming we give you the necessary IAM roles and CIDRs.
[07:47] Liam: typically 3-7 business days for a dev pilot if we have all the info: CIDRs, subnets, IAM role, and certs. production onboarding takes longer.
[07:58] Tomás: we have a transit gateway + VPN to our on-prem. if we do private endpoints in the cloud, will on-prem traffic be able to reach the endpoint through the transit?
[08:07] Liam: yes, as long as your transit routes advertise the subnets where the interface endpoints are. it's a standard TGW routing config. we'll include a sample route table.
[08:19] Raj: can we do a quick risk scenario — if one region suffers an outage, what's the degrade path?
[08:25] Liam: by default we don't fail over outside pinned regions; we can configure cross-region failover within EU to another pinned region. fallback outside EU is disallowed per your legal constraint. we can automate canary routing to test failover if you want.
[08:40] Elena: logging — request-level logs should not include raw inputs, we need redaction rules.
[08:47] Liam: we provide configurable logging at request granularity and can apply redaction rules or hashing before storage. for high security we do not store full prompts unless you opt in.
[08:59] Maya: customer question — how does billing and metering work for private?
[09:04] Maya (Redwood): metering is per-token or vcpu-minute depending on model; for private we can also do a reserved capacity contract. we'll send a pricing sheet.
[09:12] Raj: any required firewall rules on our side?
[09:15] Liam: for interface endpoints you need to allow outbound HTTPS traffic to the endpoint ENIs; for peering we need routes. we'll send a checklist.
[09:24] Tomás: what about DNS? we don't want public DNS leaking.
[09:27] Liam: you can use private hosted zones or set up split-horizon DNS. interface endpoints are reachable via private DNS names; we can provide the zone names.
[09:36] Raj: are there any known limitations with GPU model sizes or sequence lengths when running in-region?
[09:42] Liam: larger model families require specific GPU SKUs; we will surface compatible instance types for each model. sequence length: typical support up to 8k tokens for some variants, but we will confirm per-model.
[09:55] Elena: pen test evidence — can you provide a summary and contacts?
[09:59] Maya: yes we'll include sanitized reports and a contact for security_questions@redwood.example (note: placeholder) in the pack.
[10:08] Raj: ok next steps?
[10:11] Maya: summarize: 1) we'll send security pack + SOC2 docs 2) liam will prepare perf checklist and recommended instance types 3) stonecove to send CIDRs, TGW info, and a list of required subnets 4) schedule a pilot kickoff for early june.
[10:28] Tomás: i'll throw in the CIDR details by friday.
[10:31] Elena: i'll review the security pack and follow up with questions.
[10:35] Raj: sounds good.
[10:37] Maya: awesome, thanks all. we'll follow up with calendar invite for the pilot kickoff and the security bundle.
[10:45] Speaker 3: small note — we might want a demo of the console for RBAC before pilot.
[10:50] Maya: we can do a short console demo in the kickoff.
[10:55] -- End of meeting --
